cells.tense: The last days of this thing are in your hands right now, and your hands are steady.
cells.act: say the hard thing gently, once
cells.ask: Before this closes, say the true sentence you've been carrying about it — gently, once — to the person it belongs to, or once on paper, then let it lie.
cells.core:
You can hold the whole of something you've loved and still see it clearly. Where people gather around meaning, you read the room and the moment and what will land — you feel it all moving and you don't flinch from any of it. Most people would look away. You look. That's why the things you make tend to hold.

Something is finishing now. Before it closes, there's a sentence you've been carrying about it, and the clear-eyed half of you — the part that says what's true without bruising anyone — is exactly what this ending is asking for. Say that sentence once, gently, and stop. You don't need to check how it landed. You'll know. The ending does the rest.
cells.sheetLine: You hold the whole and don't look away.
cells.verb: carrying feeling and meaning toward what connects people
cells.place: at the point where something is finished and lets go

cells.tense: The ending is behind you and you're still driving it forward with both hands.
cells.act: move the structure one real inch
cells.ask: Name something in this ending that is genuinely done. Keep your hands off it for a week, and put that effort into one visible inch of what comes next.
cells.core:
Around what you're finishing, the line between yourself and the work has gone soft — you push, you redesign it, you carry it across the threshold after it's already on the other side. The intensity is real and it isn't fooling anyone but you. What's finished keeps getting re-opened because the feeling is still gripping, and the next thing can't start while you're braced against one that's done.

Let the done thing be done. For a week, keep your hands off it. Take the full weight of your push and put it into one real, visible inch of what's next — one call, one draft, one arrangement made. Slow and steady beats the breakthrough you've been bracing for. The inch will be enough to convince you. Left alone for seven days, the ending will finish itself.
cells.sheetLine: The ending's done and you're still pushing it.

cells.tense: Your hand is still on the door of this ending, long after it closed behind you.
cells.ask: Write the next three moves after this ending in plain order — first, second, third, one line each — and take step one within the week.
cells.core:
Nothing is coming through you toward what connects people right now. You know the ending is here, you can name it, and you still live on the near side of it — not moved in, not gone, holding a position in a room that started without you. The feeling is there but it doesn't reach anybody, and the closeness you'd usually make with it stays unmade.

Rather than pushing emotion into a space that's gone silent, get sharp. Take the ending you're beside and think it through fast and cleanly: what comes after it, the next three moves, the shortest honest version. Put them down one line each. Take the first move inside the week. That's the whole act — no feeling required, and none is going to be asked of you. Do it and the room you're actually in will catch up to you.

cells.tense: You're already finishing what connects these people and filing it under how things went.
cells.act: calibrate what you say to what can be heard
cells.ask: The next time you fix or close something for someone here, notice the fixing is yours before you move — then do it, or hold back. Both count.
cells.core:
You keep bringing people back to the thing that matters — the sentence that reframes a fight, the question that opens the room, the small ceremony at the end of a hard night. Ask, and you'd call it just talking, or say the group already had that tone. It had it because you set it. The hand is on the wheel. You don't count the turns as yours.

So let a turn count. The next time you speak into a gathering or close something hard with softness, know it's you calibrating what to say to what can be heard — hold that a beat before you move. Then do it, or hold back instead. Either is yours. Standing beside your own hand is the whole of it, and it doesn't need anyone to see. Once you catch yourself doing it, you'll stop misplacing it.
cells.sheetLine: The hand that keeps them talking is yours.
